channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Early-stage breast cancer gains first newly approved hormone therapy in more than 20 years
item.description: For the first time in more than two decades, the FDA has approved a new hormone therapy for early-stage breast cancer, marking a monumental shift in how the most common form of the disease is treated.

item.title: A doctor's take on the US losing measles elimination status
item.description: For many physicians of my generation, measles was a disease we rarely—or never—saw in practice. That was a sign of how well vaccination and public health efforts had worked.

item.title: Drones could soon fly blood, defibrillators and medicine to patients
item.description: Paramedics in one Florida county may soon be able to call in a drone to bring blood to a patient who's bleeding heavily.

item.title: Disrupting a developing brain circuit in adolescence may have lasting social effects
item.description: Adolescence is often described as a turbulent period of life marked by growing independence, changing social relationships and unpredictable shifts in behavior. According to researchers, tweens' and teens' behavioral changes reflect a brain that is still actively developing, yet scientists know surprisingly little about the neural mechanisms that shape social behavior during this critical stage of life.

item.title: England shows widest socioeconomic gap in frailty among 31 countries
item.description: Older adults from disadvantaged socioeconomic backgrounds experience greater levels of frailty, with England showing the biggest gap between socioeconomic groups among the 31 countries studied.

item.title: Prior authorization limits help expand opioid addiction treatment where approvals were a frequent roadblock, study finds
item.description: State laws limiting prior authorization requirements for opioid use disorder medications were associated with increased buprenorphine use in Medicaid, but only in states where those requirements were frequent barriers to access, according to a new study led by University of Michigan researchers.

item.title: FDA approves bezuclastinib in combination with sunitinib as new second-line therapy for patients with GIST
item.description: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved a combination of bezuclastinib plus sunitinib as second-line therapy after first-line treatment with imatinib for adults with advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST) based on evidence from the phase 3 PEAK study led by Dana-Farber Cancer Institute showing that the combination outperformed standard therapy with sunitinib alone.

item.title: Reducing or quitting smoking linked to lower risk for developing psoriasis
item.description: Smoking reduction is associated with a reduced risk for developing psoriasis, including psoriasis vulgaris (PsV) and palmoplantar pustulosis (PPP), according to a research letter published online Nov. 18 in JAMA Dermatology.

item.title: Inflammatory bowel disease linked to increased risk for cirrhosis
item.description: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), especially ulcerative colitis, is associated with an increased risk for cirrhosis diagnosis, according to a study recently published in Sage Open Chronic Diseases.

item.title: FDA approves Nelkarmi for ALK-positive non-small cell lung cancer
item.description: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has granted approval to Nelkarmi (neladalkib), a kinase inhibitor, for adults with locally advanced or metastatic anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK)-positive non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) who were previously treated. The approval was granted to Nuvalent and GSK.

item.title: Common patterns of b/tsDMARD use identified in rheumatoid arthritis
item.description: Common patterns of biologic and targeted synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (b/tsDMARD) use are seen among patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), and these patterns are associated with underlying genetic associations, according to a study published online Nov. 20 in Arthritis & Rheumatology.

item.title: How methylmercury impairs forebrain inhibitory circuits and induces abnormal behavior in mice
item.description: Global efforts have sought to reduce mercury pollution, but methylmercury (MeHg) remains a persistent environmental hazard that bioaccumulates in aquatic food chains. Humans are exposed to MeHg primarily through contaminated seafood. Minamata disease, officially recognized in Japan in 1956, demonstrated the devastating neurological consequences of MeHg poisoning. Since then, researchers have investigated its neurotoxic effects, including sensory, motor and psychiatric symptoms. Despite clinical reports of behavioral disturbances in people affected by MeHg poisoning, the neural circuits underlying these abnormalities remain poorly understood.

item.title: HIV viral control is necessary but not sufficient for healthy aging
item.description: Individuals with HIV show signs of faster biological aging compared with people without HIV. In other words, indicators of bodily functions that can be measured in the blood appear more like those of an older individual than those of someone the same age.

item.title: Doctors report less burnout in practices they rate as efficient, even during long workweeks
item.description: When it comes to physician burnout, how you spend your working hours may matter more than how many hours you work.

item.title: Novel metric accurately distinguishes metastasis from an independent primary tumor
item.description: Research has found that the newly developed Clonal Relatedness Index (CRI) can accurately determine whether tumors in the same patient share a common clonal origin. The findings, detailed in an article appearing in The Journal of Molecular Diagnostics, have important implications for the clinical management of complex cases of cancers of the digestive system and abdominal lining, specifically gastrointestinal, hepatopancreatobiliary and peritoneal carcinomas.

item.title: Low vitamin D could be keeping you up at night
item.description: Tossing and turning at night? The problem might not be your mattress—it could be your vitamin D levels.

item.title: How antibody therapy reverses type 1 diabetes in mice
item.description: Researchers at UC Davis Health have uncovered key mechanisms behind an experimental antibody that reverses type 1 diabetes (T1D) in mice. Findings from their study, published in the journal Diabetes, could advance efforts to develop treatments for patients with acute T1D.

item.title: Smarter EHR alerts increase use of first-line antibiotics for patients with penicillin allergy labels
item.description: Researchers at Vanderbilt Health successfully redesigned electronic health record (EHR) pop-up alerts that appear when clinicians prescribe antibiotics to patients with penicillin allergies. This adjustment significantly reduced alarm notifications for clinicians and safely provided more patients with first-line antibiotics, cephalosporins, despite their untested penicillin allergies.

item.title: Biotech firm predicts its antibody injections could compete with COVID vaccines
item.description: A biotech company yesterday announced that its lab-grown antibodies may provide an alternative to COVID vaccines.

item.title: Textile electrodes could bring wearable relief for menstrual pain and muscle soreness
item.description: Applying a mild electrical current through the skin is a drug-free way to manage menstrual pain and intense muscle soreness, but at-home devices that deliver the current are bulky and difficult to use effectively, and they require sticky gels. Now, scientists reporting in ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces have developed a reusable pain-relieving textile electrode that could be incorporated into clothing. In a preliminary test, the electrodes transmitted electrical stimulation through skin-care products to a person's skin.

item.title: Counting gut bacteria sheds new light on multiple sclerosis
item.description: Researchers from the Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB), Flemish Institute for Biotechnology, KU Leuven and the Belgian National MS Centre in Melsbroek have taken a significant step toward understanding the relationship between gut microbiota and multiple sclerosis (MS). This could lead to better insights and treatments in the future.

item.title: Growing miniature tumors to help personalize cancer treatment
item.description: Modern cancer care is based on many factors. Physicians use scans, lab tests and decades of clinical research to help decide which treatments are best for patients.

item.title: How persistent inflammation reprograms the immune system to promote T-cell exhaustion
item.description: When the body encounters an infection, its immune system must respond rapidly and effectively. Dendritic cells play a central role in this process. They detect pathogens, capture their components and activate specialized immune cells known as CD8 T cells, which can recognize and eliminate infected cells.

item.title: E-scooter injuries can cause lasting symptoms and work disruption
item.description: Many people treated for traumatic brain injury (TBI) after electric scooter crashes experience significant time away from work and symptoms that persist for months, according to findings published Nov. 17 in JAMA Network Open.

item.title: Cosmetic surgery is on the rise globally. Social media, celebrities reduce taboos and influence beauty ideals
item.description: Nearly 18 million cosmetic surgeries were performed worldwide in 2025, increasing by roughly 25% since 2021.

item.title: Sleeping 9 or more hours linked to a higher risk of death in people with heart disease
item.description: Adults with heart disease who sleep nine or more hours a day may be at greater risk of dying prematurely. That's the conclusion of a study published in the journal PLOS One that examined the relationship between sleep duration and mortality in more than 3,000 adults from the U.S.

item.title: The DRC's Ebola crisis revives an old ethical question: What do health workers owe patients?
item.description: The World Health Organization declared the Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak on May 15, 2026. As of Nov. 18, there have been 11,712 cases and 5,720 deaths, nearly all in the Democratic Republic of Congo, or DRC.

item.title: Pimple‑popping videos can be disgusting—and strangely satisfying
item.description: Some people relax by watching someone squeeze pus from a stranger's face. I'm one of them. I have favorite accounts, strong opinions about technique and very little patience for a video that ends before the pore has been properly cleared.

item.title: What if rheumatoid arthritis could be prevented before the pain begins?
item.description: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) begins years before someone experiences the joint pain, swelling and stiffness associated with the disease. Now, researchers at the University of Colorado Anschutz are exploring how artificial intelligence and advances in biological research could help identify the immune mechanisms underlying those early warning symptoms and signs and potentially prevent the disease before it starts.

item.title: Glucose sensors for type 2 diabetes deserve second look from NHS
item.description: A wearable sensor that allows people with type 2 diabetes using insulin to track their glucose levels in real time could prove good value for the NHS, a University of Manchester–led study suggests. The research, published in Diabetes, Obesity and Metabolism, assessed the value for money of real-time continuous glucose monitoring compared with standard finger-prick testing.
